newsitem.title: ITALY: UN wants population issue off food summit agenda. [CORRECTED 11:26 GMT 29/9]
newsitem.headline: UN wants population issue off food summit agenda. [CORRECTED 11:26 GMT 29/9]

text.p: The director-general of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said on Wednesday that he wants to keep population issues off the agenda of a global food summit in Rome.
"Food for All" is the theme of the November 13-17 FAO World Food Summit, which director-general Jacques Diouf hopes will result in an effective plan of action to fight hunger.

Diouf, during a briefing for broadcast media at the agency's Rome headquarters, cited statistics which he said pointed to a need for global discussion of food issues: 800 million people were chronically undernourished and an additional 3.6 billion people would need to be fed by the year 2030.
Population growth is a major factor in food security but Diouf said he did not want the summit to address an issue that has steeped other U.N. conferences in controversy.
"I hope that we will not reopen the debate into what has already been decided at the Cairo conference," he said. "This (summit) is to supplement what has already been decided".
The U.N. population conference in Cairo in 1994 was dominated by a contentious abortion debate which pitted the Vatican and the United States against each other.

Among its conclusions was that unsafe abortion was a major public health concern and that were abortion was not against the law it should be safe. (Corrects by deleting erroneous reference to parental consent.)

A FAO source, however, said population issues were among sticking points that had arisen when country delegations met in Rome this week to decide on the wording of the food summit's policy statement. The summit will be opened by Pope John Paul.
"Those opposed to the Cairo conference see it as a way to roll back the wording while those in favour see it as an opportunity to break new ground," the source said.

Diouf said about 100 heads of state and government had confirmed they would attend during the final two days of the summit. He declined to give names for security reasons. Among those invited is Cuban President Fidel Castro.
"The objective of the summit is to raise the awareness of the problem of food security of world leaders and the public in general," he said. "We expect awareness will lead to action."
Responding to a question about criticism of U.N. spending, Diouf said FAO was committed to containing costs and organising the summit "as efficiently as possible".
As an example, he said the summit was being held at FAO headquarters to eliminate travel and hotel spending for staff.
The FAO source said the agency had also asked delegations to keep the number of people sent to Rome to a minimum and not to plan any lavish receptions and parties during the summit.
"We want it to be a low-key and austere event," the source said.
